newsitem.title: POLAND: Buoyant zloty set to challenge central bank cap.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant zloty set to challenge central bank cap.

text.p: Foreign inflows into Polish treasuries and privatisations will keep the zloty charged this week and push it into battle with currency-buying central bank interventions, following a pattern set on Monday, dealers said.

"Foreigners sold currencies and the zloty nearly hit 1.6 percent from parity today before the central bank intervened... with privatisation inflows keeping the zloty buoyant this week," said Mateusz Bieniek of Societe Generale in Warsaw.
The National Bank of Poland (NBP) bought some $45 million on Monday when the zloty remained above key resistance at 1.5 percent from parity for a lengthy period of time, dealers said.
The zloty closed at 1.53/1.49 percent from the trading band centre, stronger than Friday's 1.51/1.46 percent finish.
It closed at 3.2390/00 to the dollar, down from 3.2385/95 on Friday and at 1.8703/13 to the mark, up from 1.8714/25.
The NBP bought dollars at 3.2395 and 3.2405 zlotys, or when the zloty was some 1.55 to 1.53 percent from parity.
Dealers said the NBP's post-trade zloty fixing at 1.49 percent, weaker than the market close, signalled the bank was willing to again defend 1.5 percent from parity if necessary.
Foreign inflows into Bank Handlowy SA's one billion zloty IPO were seen as the zloty's main source of strength this week.
"The zloty will most probably run into a ceiling created by central bank action this week with the market remaining long on currencies," said Jerzy Wyjadlowski from Bank Slaski SA.
Analysts said Polish interest rates should remain on hold despite better-than-expected May inflation, which rose just 0.6 percent last month against expectations of 0.9 percent growth.
Year-on-year CPI fell to 14.6 percent from April's 15.3.

"Interest rates will not be reduced just because inflation is falling because lower rates would create quicker growth of money supply and lead to a price growth impulse," said Jacek Lech, deputy chief dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
"Credit growth also has to slow ahead of any interest rate move, which is not expected in the next 2-3 months," he added.

Minimum prices of all T-bills fell at Monday's primary auction on total demand of 1.226 billion zlotys against a 1.4 billion zloty offer. The benchmark 52-week paper average yield increased to 21.49 percent, below market expectations at 21.55.
The ministry will offer an additional 600 million zlotys of 52-week T-bills at its next primary tender on June 18.
On the money market one-day rates eased as the central bank refrained from staging any open market operations on Monday, dealers said.
Overnight rates closed at 21.60/21.90 percent, down from the opening's 22.05/22.15, while tomorrow/next depos were at 21.85/22.05 percent, down from 21.95/22.15.
